Important new evidence•Peer-reviewed prospective cohort study•October 7, 2026

Sweet-tooth preference tracks with higher dementia risk

In a prospective UK Biobank analysis, a sweet-tooth preference profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk than a health-aligned profile; the observational design does not show that changing preference prevents dementia.

Key quantitative results: Compared with the health-aligned profile, the sweet-tooth profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk.

ManagementRisk reduction

Added October 8, 2026 · DOI:10.1007/s11357-026-02567-3; PMID:42842075

Evidence summaryDesign, results, and what changed

Thirty-second field brief

The study links a preference for sweet foods—not measured intake—to future dementia and to three biological-aging measures, with stronger joint risk among people with high genetic susceptibility. The effect sizes are sizeable, but residual confounding, selection, reverse causation and imperfect translation from preference to consumption prevent causal or prescriptive claims. Biological-aging markers explained only a small share of the association.

Study design

Investigators used UK Biobank food-preference questionnaires to derive health-aligned, broad-preference and sweet-tooth profiles by latent profile analysis. Cox models related profiles to incident all-cause, Alzheimer and vascular dementia and tested interaction with genetic risk. Linear models assessed KDM biological-age acceleration, PhenoAge acceleration and leukocyte telomere length; mediation analyses were exploratory.

Key quantitative results

  • Compared with the health-aligned profile, the sweet-tooth profile was associated with 79% higher all-cause dementia risk, 62% higher Alzheimer disease risk and 202% higher vascular-dementia risk.
  • The sweet-tooth profile was also associated with faster Klemera-Doubal biological-age and PhenoAge acceleration and shorter leukocyte telomere length. A significant additive interaction indicated greater combined dementia risk with high genetic susceptibility.
  • Exploratory mediation analyses estimated that the three biological-aging measures statistically accounted for only 2.28%-4.82% of the observed diet-preference association, leaving most of the association unexplained.

What changed

The cohort adds prospective, profile-based evidence connecting sweet-food preference, genetic susceptibility, multiple biological-aging measures and dementia subtypes in one analysis.

Strength of evidence

Moderate observational evidence for association, supported by prospective follow-up, time-to-event analysis and convergent aging measures. It is insufficient for causality or a treatment recommendation because exposure was preference rather than intake, confounding and reverse causation remain possible, and mediation was exploratory.

Clinical and field impactInterpretation, implementation, and access

Clinical significance

The findings are consistent with counseling toward established healthy dietary patterns as part of multidomain risk reduction, but they do not justify genetic testing, a sweet-food cutoff or a claim that changing food preferences will prevent Alzheimer disease.

Field medical relevance

Relevant to risk-reduction discussions and prevention-study design, particularly questions about diet-genetic interaction and whether biological-aging measures explain dementia associations.

Access or reimbursement relevance

The study creates no authorization, availability, guideline endorsement, reimbursement or coverage change. Its implications concern prevention research and counseling context rather than access to a specific product or service.

Likely questionsWhat you may hear and what the evidence supports
Does a sweet tooth cause Alzheimer disease?
The study shows association, not causation. Food preference is not the same as measured intake, and unmeasured confounding or preclinical disease could contribute.
Should APOE or polygenic testing be ordered to target dietary counseling?
No clinical-testing recommendation follows from this observational interaction analysis. Risk counseling should rely on established guidance and individual context.
Did biological aging explain most of the association?
No. The exploratory mediators accounted for only 2.28%-4.82%, so most of the association was not explained by those measures.
Critique and limitationsBias, uncertainty, and missing evidence
  • Observational UK Biobank design with healthy-volunteer selection
  • Food preference rather than objectively measured consumption
  • Residual confounding and reverse causation cannot be excluded
  • Genetic interaction and mediation analyses do not establish clinical utility
  • Biological-aging measures explained only a small proportion of the association
  • No randomized evidence that changing preference reduces dementia incidence

Primary source · DOI · PubMed record

Sun M, Huang F, Sun N, et al. Dietary preference, biological aging, and incident dementia: a prospective cohort study. Geroscience. Published online October 7, 2026. doi:10.1007/s11357-026-02567-3.
